title: Context, Tokens, and Modalities
summary: This intermediate module enables learners to distinguish context, tokens, and modalities when examining an AI system. After completing it, learners can identify unsupported assumptions about token counting, context limits, and multimodal input.
objectives: Distinguish a token from a word, character, or modality.
Explain how a sequence of tokens represents context for a model.
Classify text and images as modalities without assuming that each modality has a universal token cost.
Recognize when an exact context limit or token count is UNKNOWN for an unspecified system.
Evaluate an input by separating its information type from its model-specific representation.

sections.title: Source correction
paragraphs: The prior cited entry was content/modules/ai-foundations/context-tokens-and-modalities.json. It was due for review because it was attributed to an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. That local path was removed from the source list and replaced by canonical arXiv records available over HTTPS.

The source change affects the provenance supporting two parts of the module: the explanation of token sequences and the explanation of paired text and image modalities. The instructional scope remains limited to context, tokens, and modalities. No system-specific context limit, version, configuration key, or counting rule has been added.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that the learner already understands that a model receives input and produces output, but it explains the relevant representation concepts without requiring advanced mathematics.

The module is provider-neutral. Exact context limits, tokenization rules, and multimodal accounting methods are UNKNOWN for an unspecified system, so no universal figures or system-specific procedures are asserted.

sections.title: Tokens and context
paragraphs: A token is a unit in the sequence a model processes. Tokens are converted into numerical representations before they move through a transformer. A token should not be treated as universally equivalent to one word or one character because sequence construction depends on the method used to divide and represent input.

Context is the information made available to the model through its input representation for a particular operation. In a text sequence, earlier and later token positions can be related through attention. The usefulness of a piece of context depends both on whether it is represented in the input and on how the model uses that representation.

An exact token count cannot be inferred safely from a visual inspection of words or characters. It must come from the counting rules of the particular system being evaluated. Without an identified system and its documentation, the exact count and maximum supported context are UNKNOWN.
sections.callout: Do not substitute a word count for a token count unless the identified system explicitly defines them as equivalent.

sections.title: Modalities
paragraphs: A modality is a form of information, such as text or images. A modality describes what kind of information is supplied. A token describes a unit in the representation processed by a model. These terms answer different questions and are not interchangeable.

Research on learning from paired natural-language and image data demonstrates that text and images can participate in one learning task while retaining their different forms. This supports describing such a system as multimodal, but it does not establish one universal method for counting every image or text input.

The computational representation and input cost of a modality depend on the particular system. An image must not be assumed to equal one token, and its cost must not be derived from its file count alone. For an unspecified system, the conversion and accounting rules are UNKNOWN.

sections.title: A provider-neutral analysis workflow
paragraphs: First, identify each input modality. For example, classify prose as text and a picture as an image. Second, separate the original information from its model representation. Words, characters, image dimensions, files, and tokens are related only through system-specific processing rules.

Third, determine whether the system and its documented counting method are known. If they are not known, report the exact token count and context limit as UNKNOWN rather than guessing. Fourth, evaluate relevance separately from size. Information can fit within an input representation yet still be irrelevant, ambiguous, or poorly placed.

This workflow lets a learner do something more precise than simply calling all input context. The learner can now state which inputs are modalities, which quantities are representation units, and which conclusions require system-specific evidence.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a token from a modality?
choices: A token is a form of information, while a modality is always one word.
A modality is a form of information, while a token is a unit in a model's input sequence representation.
A token and a modality are interchangeable names for every input.
Every image is one modality and therefore exactly one token.
questions.explanation: The module defines a modality as a form of information, such as text or images, and a token as a unit in the sequence representation processed by a model.

questions.prompt: What should an analyst report when asked for the exact context limit of an unspecified system?
choices: A limit inferred from the number of words
A limit copied from any other system
UNKNOWN until the particular system and its documented rules are identified
questions.explanation: The module states that exact context limits and counting rules are system-specific and are UNKNOWN when no particular system is identified.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion about an image input is supported by this module?
choices: Every image always consumes one token.
An image's representation cost can always be derived from its file count.
An image is a modality, while its representation and accounting depend on the particular system.
Images cannot be used with text in the same learning task.
questions.explanation: The module distinguishes an image modality from its computational representation and states that representation and accounting rules depend on the particular system.

questions.prompt: What did the source correction change?
choices: It added a universal context limit.
It replaced an unverified local source entry with canonical HTTPS arXiv records supporting token-sequence and text-image modality explanations.
It introduced a system-specific configuration key.
It established that every word is one token.
questions.explanation: The source-correction section states that the unverified local entry was replaced by canonical arXiv records and identifies the affected explanations.
